title: Are Your AI-Reflection Questions Undermining Reflection
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Dempsey continues his series on replacing reflection prompts with metacognitive questions drawn from solution-focused brief therapy, here covering seven ways teachers accidentally slip back into reflection mode when asking students about their AI use. Each mistake is paired with why it breaks the metacognitive frame and a concrete alternative question. The mistakes include asking what students learned, adding a meta-reflection layer, making the observer the teacher, demanding too much detail, inviting self-judgment, turning discoveries into mandates, and holding a predetermined right answer. He argues the common fix is subtractive: remove what was added and trust the questions to work by simply existing. The piece is practical for teachers designing AI-use assignments, though it rests on the earlier posts in the series for its rationale.
points: Questions that ask students to summarise, justify or judge their AI use return performance and platitudes rather than awareness.
A neutral, non-evaluative observer, such as a classmate or future self, preserves the distance that lets students notice what is working.
Asking for one concrete instance beats demanding comprehensive documentation of unconscious decisions, which produces fabricated rationalisation.
Mandating a strategy a student discovered removes the ownership that made it valuable, and having a right answer in mind invalidates their noticing.
quotes: Most decisions about AI use happen intuitively, unconsciously, reactively. Forcing students to narrate every micro-decision creates fabricated rationalization.

Why it breaks metacognition: You’ve collapsed the external perspective into teacher-pleasing. The whole point of observer questions is to create distance from the student’s own anxiety and self-judgment.
Why it breaks metacognition: You’ve taken their self-discovery and tried to codify it as a requirement. This removes the agency and ownership that made the discovery valuable in the first place.

In solution-focused work, the student’s identification is valid because it’s theirs. There’s no “correct” exception to notice, no “right” resource to identify. Whatever they notice that works for them is the intervention.
Why it breaks metacognition: “What did you learn?” is abstract and retrospective. It asks students to summarize, when our goal is only to notice patterns (even if they’re hypothetical).
